rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / CLASSES / CHAPTER 12

slides.title: Classes
slides.main: A class combines data and the actions on it into one type.

items.title: Class
items.sub: A blueprint: objects-instances are made from it

items.title: Methods
items.sub: Functions in a class; self is the object

items.title: Output
items.sub: How an object is shown to a person

body.text: String, list, dict are classes too; now we make our own types.

slides.title: Class and object
slides.sub: The blueprint and what is made from it
slides.main: One class, any number of instances, each living on its own.

body.text:
class Dog:
    pass

d = Dog()
print(type(d))
print(isinstance(d, Dog))
Class names start with a capital: that tells them from functions.

slides.title: Constructor and attributes
slides.sub: __init__ is called when an object is created
slides.main: The constructor guarantees: every object is born in good order.

slides.title: Methods
slides.main: Data and actions together: read the class to understand the object.

slides.title: What self is
slides.sub: The object the method was called on
slides.main: One method for all, but each instance has its own data.

body.text:
class Counter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.value = 0
    def inc(self):
        self.value += 1

a = Counter()
b = Counter()
a.inc()
print(a.value, b.value)
Counter.inc(a)      # same as a.inc()
print(a.value)

slides.title: Class and instance attributes
slides.sub: Shared by all, and one's own
slides.main: Create mutable data in __init__, not at class level.

body.text:
class Dog:
    legs = 4                  # shared
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name      # own

a, b = Dog("A"), Dog("B")
print(a.legs, b.legs, Dog.legs)

class Bad:
    items = []                # trap: one list for all

x, y = Bad(), Bad()
x.items.append(1)
print(y.items)

slides.title: Objects and references
slides.main: An object is a package with an address: two names can point to one instance.

body.text:
class Box:
    def __init__(self, v):
        self.v = v

a = Box(1)
b = a              # one object, two names
b.v = 99
print(a.v)
print(Box(1) == Box(1))
== compares the objects themselves, not their data: we'll customize it next chapter.

slides.title: __str__ and __repr__
slides.sub: How an object looks in print and in the console
slides.main: __str__ is for people, __repr__ is for developers.

slides.title: Encapsulation
slides.sub: The class guards its own rules
slides.main: One underscore means internal, hands off; changes go through methods.

slides.title: Objects in collections
slides.sub: Lists and dicts with meaningful items
slides.main: All you know about lists and dicts still works; the items are just richer.

slides.title: How to design a class
slides.sub: Nouns are classes, verbs are methods
slides.main: Outside, only clear operations show; how it works inside you need not know.

slides.title: Typical mistakes
slides.main: A method needs self in its header, and an attribute inside is always self.name.

body.text:
class A:
    def hello():        # self forgotten
        return "hi"

A().hello()
TypeError: A.hello() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given
Also: _init_ for __init__, a class-level list, a method without (), a typo in an attribute name.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: A class is a type blueprint, an object is an instance; init sets data, self is the object.
